summary: Oakridge Capital is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for predictable, reserved GPU capacity to serve low-latency, high-throughput financial inference workloads. Key concerns: data isolation, SOC2/KMS, burst strategy to handle end-of-month peaks, autoscaling behavior, and cost tradeoffs between reserved vs hosted burst. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Oakridge Head of ML), Mariana Ruiz (CTO), Samir Khan (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): Oakridge exploring reserved GPUs, isolation, burst to hosted, quantization and batching strategies, SOC2 docs requested.

00:00 - Sofia Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm sofia with redwood inference, joining today is marcus our solutions eng, we're here to learn about oakridge's workloads and see if dedicated makes sense
00:22 - Ethan Cole: hey so thanks, quick context, we're a quant trading infra team, doing realtime inference for risk and signal scoring, mostly running internal LLMs for doc parsing and alerts, latency is critical, and all data must remain in our network
00:40 - Mariana Ruiz: yeah, data residency + isolation are non-negotiable given regs, so we're evaluating private vs dedicated, but want to understand cost/throughput tradeoffs
01:05 - Marcus Lee: sounds good. quick Q on scale — what's your baseline and peak? qps, model sizes, and what hardware you're on today?
01:20 - Samir Khan: baseline is ~60 qps, spikes up to 450 qps at end-of-day and end-of-month windows. models are a mixture; 7b and 13b variants, mostly LLaMA-derived, we currently run on on-prem cluster with A100s and a couple of older 80GB machines
01:45 - Ethan Cole: we also do synchronous scoring, p95 latency target is <200ms for single-turn scoring, some batching for bulk jobs is ok but customer-facing paths need sub-150ms ideally
02:10 - Sofia Patel: got it. ok redwood dedicate — we do reserved GPU pools that you can isolate to your tenancy, with optional private control plane for VPCs. the key configs are nodes reserved, autoscaling policies, and a burst path if you want to overflow to hosted capacity
02:35 - Mariana Ruiz: quick clarification — burst to hosted, does that mean data leaves our VPC? security team will flag that unless traffic is encrypted and we have controls
02:48 - Marcus Lee: good question — burst is done over customer-configured peering and TLS, we can do VPC peering or private link; for highly regulated customers we recommend an on-prem/private deployment. for dedicated we support KMS integration, audit logs, and can sign an addendum for data handling
03:10 - Samir Khan: ok, but if we reserve say 8 gpus and we hit 450 qps, what's the expected latency delta when bursting? and do we get consistent kernel choices so results don't change?
03:30 - Marcus Lee: latency will depend on model and batch shapes. for example on 8xA100 for a 13b quantized model, with continuous batching and prefix KV cache tuning we expect ~120-180ms p95 for single-turn workloads. when bursting to hosted, you're likely hitting a different instance type and may see up to 1.5x variance in p95 unless we pin to compatible model variants and quant profiles
04:05 - Ethan Cole: pinning is important — we can't have inference drift between environments, produce different tokenization or sampling differences
04:20 - Marcus Lee: we do model version pinning and provide a compatible model variant policy — automatic fallback only to verified variants to avoid output drift. also we log inference hashes and outputs for debugging (audit logs)
04:42 - Mariana Ruiz: you mentioned KMS, can you support our HSM-backed keys? and are there SOC2 / ISO certification docs?
04:55 - Sofia Patel: yes we have SOC2 reports and can share network diagrams. KMS integrations include AWS KMS and customer HSM integrations via our private control plane; we'll attach the security pack in the follow-up
05:12 - Samir Khan: how does your autoscaler behave? we need predictable throughput not just cost-savings — e.g. scale up lead-time, whether scaling is reactive or predictive, min-reserved capacity during maintenance windows
05:30 - Marcus Lee: our Dedicated autoscaler supports reserve counts (min nodes), target utilisation policies, and burst to preapproved capacity. scaling can be reactive but we also offer scheduled scaling windows and warm pools to eliminate cold start. if you want near-zero warmup we recommend reserved + warm pool with the burst path kept as emergency overflow
06:00 - Ethan Cole: can you explain warm pools vs pre-warming? we need to avoid long KV cache misses on scale events
06:18 - Marcus Lee: warm pools keep model processes resident on GPU but not necessarily fully warmed KV caches; pre-warming applies a workload replay to populate caches. for financial workloads we usually do a small pre-warm traffic set at the start of peak windows to prime KV caches
06:35 - Ethan Cole: that makes sense. what's typical sizing guidance — how many A100s per 100 qps for 13b quantized?
06:50 - Marcus Lee: rough rule: a single 80GB A100 can sustain ~40-80 qps for 13b quantized depending on seq length and batch tuning. so for 450 qps you'd be looking at ~6-12 GPUs with aggressive batching; for more conservative low-latency profiles plan for more GPUs to reduce queueing
07:15 - Samir Khan: cost question — is it cheaper to reserve 12 GPUs or reserve 6 and burst to hosted for peaks? our finance team will want clear burn rate numbers
07:30 - Sofia Patel: depends on utilization — reserved gets predictability and isolation; burst reduces committed spend but adds some latency variance and potential egress/network costs. we'll send a comparative spreadsheet with unit costs and example scenarios
07:48 - Mariana Ruiz: we have compliance folks who will ask about audit logs retention and SSO/SAML integration — how fine-grained is your RBAC?
08:00 - Marcus Lee: RBAC is role-based with route-level permissions, SSO via SAML/OIDC, and we keep audit logs with configurable retention; longer retention is an add-on. can provide sample policies we've implemented for banks
08:20 - Ethan Cole: for the POC, we're thinking about a 2-week bench: start with mirrored traffic for a subset of flows, measure p95, throughput, and cost. can redwood run a side-by-side benchmark?
08:35 - Marcus Lee: yes, we can do a POC where we provision a small dedicated pool (2-4 GPUs) and then run a scaled benchmark with your prompts. we'll capture token-level latency, cost per token, and p95. we'll also test a burst scenario to hosted to measure delta
08:52 - Sofia Patel: action wise we'll send pricing and security pack, and marcus will propose the benchmark plan. samir to share infra telemetry. target to kick off next week
09:05 - Mariana Ruiz: question on model compilation/quant — do you support int8/4 quant and will outputs differ from fp16?
09:20 - Marcus Lee: we support a spectrum of quant strategies and we evaluate quality/regression against your eval sets. int8/4 can change outputs slightly; we run a regression check and recommend the highest quant that meets accuracy SLO; for high-risk flows we keep fp16 or conservative quant
09:45 - Ethan Cole: ok, that answers it. any limitations on libraries or custom kernels? we use some custom ops in-house
09:55 - Marcus Lee: we can bring custom kernels into the runtime but it requires an onboarding step; if it's critical for you we can include that in the POC scope and run compatibility tests
10:15 - Samir Khan: how do you handle model updates and rollouts? we need canary deploys and quick rollbacks
10:28 - Marcus Lee: we support canary rollouts, A/B traffic splits by route, and automatic fallback policies if latency or error rate thresholds are breached. rollbacks are immediate and we keep previous model artifacts available for quick redeploy
10:45 - Sofia Patel: also worth mentioning intelligent batching/caching suggestions in Redwood Optimize — it will propose batch sizes and cache TTLs to hit your latency targets while reducing token costs
11:05 - Ethan Cole: one more: what about telemetry — can we get token-level latency by route and trace into our existing observability (datadog/newrelic)?
11:18 - Marcus Lee: yes we expose per-route metrics and traces; we have integrations for Datadog, New Relic, and you can ingest logs into your SIEM via S3 or streaming endpoints
11:35 - Mariana Ruiz: security-wise, our legal will want a network diagram and data flow, plus the SOC2 report; please include the redaction and data retention policies
11:50 - Sofia Patel: noted, we'll include network diagrams and the security pack. also, if you prefer private deployment, we can discuss on-prem package pricing vs dedicated with strict VPC peering
12:10 - Samir Khan: about the autoscaler again — in maintenance windows we can't allow scale-ins that drop below a min throughput. can you pin min capacity by time window?
12:25 - Marcus Lee: yes, scheduled scaling policies and min node counts are supported; we can also set grace periods and warm pool sizes to keep throughput constant during maintenance
12:42 - Ethan Cole: what's the usual SLA for Dedicated — uptime and p95 latency guarantees?
12:55 - Sofia Patel: Dedicated has an SLA for instance availability and best-effort latency SLOs; we can discuss custom SLAs for enterprise contracts — typically uptime >99.9% and we commit to throughput targets based on reserved capacity
13:12 - Mariana Ruiz: final question for now: contractual and procurement timeline — we need to present to procurement next week, are you flexible on contract terms for pilot?
13:28 - Sofia Patel: yes, for pilots we usually do a short-term agreement; procurement can review standard terms and we'll include an addendum for security controls they require
13:45 - Ethan Cole: great. to recap: you'll send pricing and security docs, marcus sends POC plan, samir shares telemetry; we'll aim to kick off POC week of 3/9
14:05 - Sofia Patel: perfect, thanks all. marcus, any final technical notes?
14:12 - Marcus Lee: just that we'll include quant/regression test steps and a checklist for warm pools and pre-warm traffic. I'll include estimated GPU counts for different latency profiles in the plan
14:25 - Mariana Ruiz: thanks, talk soon
14:30 - Meeting ended

Notes on transcript quality: some product names may be transcribed incorrectly (e.g., 'Dedicate' instead of Dedicated, 'K V cash' instead of KV cache). occasional speaker mislabels.
